screens.heading: Read it like an investigator

teacher.say: Hover over or tap each part of this fake email. Every part is a clue.

body: Treat a suspicious email as evidence. Instead of asking whether it feels right, check its parts one by one. Hover over or tap each part below to see what an investigator would look at.

parts.label: From
parts.title: The sender address
parts.check: Look at the real address, not the display name. The domain examplebank-secure.co is not the bank's own domain. It only borrows the name.

parts.label: Subject
parts.title: The subject line
parts.check: Capital letters and a deadline are meant to rush you. Real organisations rarely threaten you in a subject line.

parts.title: The greeting
parts.check: Your bank knows your name. A vague greeting suggests a template sent to thousands of people.

parts.text: We noticed unusual activity. Confirm your details within 24 hours or your account will be closed.
parts.title: The request
parts.check: An unexpected threat with a deadline is a pressure lever. A real provider would not close your account over an email you did not expect.

parts.caption: Opens: https://examplebank-secure.co/confirm
parts.title: The link
parts.check: Hover over a link before clicking. The destination is the same lookalike domain and leads to a sign-in page.

parts.caption: Compressed archive, 2.4 MB
parts.title: The attachment
parts.check: You did not ask for a statement, and a compressed archive is a common way to carry malware. Do not open it.

screens.key_takeaway: Every part of an email is a clue: sender, greeting, request, link and attachment.

screens.heading: Start with the sender

teacher.say: The sender line is the easiest thing to fake and the easiest thing to check.

body: The name shown at the top of an email is just text that the sender chose. The address inside the angle brackets is what matters.

points.label: Display name versus address
points.text: Anyone can type any display name. Check the address every time, especially on a phone, where only the name is shown by default.

points.label: Lookalike domains
points.text: Watch for extra words (examplebank-secure.co), swapped characters (examp1ebank.com, where the number 1 replaces the letter l) and different endings (.co instead of .com).

points.label: A different Reply-To
points.text: The From line can look internal while replies are sent to an outside address. If an email asks you to reply, check where the reply would go.

points.label: Real accounts that were hacked
points.text: Sometimes the sender is a real colleague whose account was taken over. If a message is out of character, confirm it through another channel.

example.title: Spot the trick
example.text: A message appears to come from 'IT Helpdesk' and the From address ends in your company's domain. Look closer: the Reply-To address ends in outlook-mail.co, so any reply, including a password, goes to an outsider.

screens.key_takeaway: Judge the real sender address, and check where replies would go.

screens.heading: Links and attachments

teacher.say: This is where most attacks actually do their damage, so slow down here.

body: The sender line gets you to open the message. The link or the file is what gives the attacker access.

points.label: Hover first
points.text: Hovering over a link shows its real destination. On a phone, press and hold. If it does not match who the message claims to be from, do not open it.

points.label: Shortened links
points.text: Link shorteners hide the destination. Treat an unexpected short link as an unknown address.

points.label: The padlock myth
points.text: The padlock only means the connection is encrypted. Fake sites use it too, so it says nothing about who runs the page.

points.label: Risky attachments
points.text: Be careful with unexpected zip archives, HTML files, and Office documents that ask you to enable editing or macros.

points.label: Go direct
points.text: Instead of using a link, open the website yourself with a bookmark or by typing the address.

screens.key_takeaway: Do not trust a link or a file you did not expect. Reach the real site yourself.

screens.heading: Tone and content

teacher.say: Here is a surprise: a perfectly written email can still be a trap.

body: Beyond technical clues, ask what the message wants from you and how it is trying to make you feel.

points.label: Pressure
points.text: Deadlines, threats and warnings of closure are designed to stop you from thinking.

points.label: Unusual requests
points.text: Gift cards, changed bank details, passwords, one-time codes and urgent payments are things a legitimate sender rarely asks for by email.

points.label: Generic greetings
points.text: Phrases like Dear customer are common in mass mailings. A personal name alone does not prove anything, though.

points.label: Too good or too bad
points.text: Surprise prizes, refunds and sudden legal trouble are classic bait.

points.label: Perfect polish
points.text: Good spelling and a professional design no longer prove an email is real. Modern tools can produce polished text for any scam.

screens.key_takeaway: Judge what the message asks you to do, not how professional it looks.

screens.heading: The 30-second check

teacher.say: Pass the quiz after this and Spot the phish unlocks. It is a great way to practise.

body: Use these questions on every unexpected message. They take about thirty seconds and turn a vague feeling into a decision.
Pass the quiz at the end of this module to unlock the Spot the phish activity, where you can practise on fake emails.

points.label: 1. Who?
points.text: Is the real sender address what I expect?

points.label: 2. What?
points.text: Is it asking for a password, money, a code or a quick favour?

points.label: 3. Where?
points.text: Where does the link really go, and could I reach the site myself?

points.label: 5. Verify
points.text: If I am still unsure, I check through a separate channel I already know, then report it.

screens.key_takeaway: When in doubt, check separately, then report.
